Say what a random slope frees, and check *before you fit it* whether your covariate varies enough **within** groups for the question to have an answer. 2. Fit `(1 + x | group)` and read the two standard deviations and the correlation out of the covariance block the engine returns. 3. Explain why the intercept–slope correlation changes, and can change sign, when you move the origin of the covariate without changing the model. 4. Compare a random-slope model against a random-intercept model with AIC and with a likelihood-ratio test, and say why the usual reference distribution is wrong when the thing you are testing is a variance. 5. Describe what shrinkage does to a group's *slope*, and say why a group with three measurements keeps only a little of the slope its own points suggest. 6. JARO is in the corridor and will be needed by the end of the hour.** **Itchy:** Last week I drew you a picture and said one sentence about it that I want back before we start. Toto. A random slope asks whether the relationship between *y* and *x* differs from group to group. Before you can ask that, *x* has to differ within a group; otherwise there is nothing for a per-bird slope to be estimated *from*, and the software will find that out about ninety seconds after you do, in a worse mood. First: which of these columns moves *within* a bird? You already have the tool. A repeatability is the share of variance that sits **between** individuals, so one minus it is the share that sits within. ::: {#within-bird .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.julia .cell-code} candidates = [:Tarsus, :BillL, :BillW, :Tail, :Weight] share_within = Dict{Symbol,Float64}() within_sd = Dict{Symbol,Float64}() @printf("%-8s %6s %8s %8s %12s\n", "column", "rows", "R", "1 - R", "within SD") for c in candidates d0 = dropmissing(sparrows, [c]) d = DataFrame(BirdID = d0.BirdID, y = Float64.(d0[!, c])) R = repeatability(drm(bf(@formula(y ~ 1 + (1|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = d)).estimate share_within[c] = 1 - R g = combine(groupby(d, :BirdID), :y => (v -> length(v) > 1 ? std(v) : missing) => :sw) within_sd[c] = mean(skipmissing(g.sw)) @printf("%-8s %6d %8.4f %8.4f %12.4f\n", c, nrow(d), R, 1 - R, within_sd[c]) end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` column rows R 1 - R within SD Tarsus 459 0.9288 0.0712 0.1644 BillL 451 0.7320 0.2680 0.2414 BillW 451 0.5176 0.4824 0.1503 Tail 446 0.6278 0.3722 1.2933 Weight 459 0.5824 0.4176 0.9907 ``` ::: ::: **Toto:** Tarsus is nearly all between. **Itchy:** Tarsus is 7\.1% within a bird and the rest between, which is Class 6's number arriving as a warning. A grown sparrow's leg bone does not change between captures, so a per-bird slope *on tarsus* asks 171 birds for the steepness of a line through points stacked on top of each other. Mass is near the other end of the table: 41\.8% of the variation in mass is a bird differing from itself. **Eddie:** Because mass is condition and tarsus is architecture. **Itchy:** Because mass is condition and tarsus is architecture, and that distinction is worth more than today's arithmetic. **Momo:** Then why mass? Bill width has a larger within-bird share than mass does. It is the largest in the table. **Itchy:** It is, and I am glad you read the whole column rather than the row I pointed at, because that is the trap in this table. **A share does not tell you what the variation is made of.** A grown sparrow's bill width is architecture too; its within-bird share is large because the trait is a couple of millimetres wide and the calipers are not that precise, so most of what moves between captures is the measuring, not the bird. Look at the two numbers together: bill width moves 48% of its variation within a bird, and that movement is 0.1503 of a millimetre. Mass genuinely changes: a sparrow is heavier after a good week and lighter after a bad one, and 0.991 grams of within-bird movement is a bird, not a ruler. **Momo:** So the rule is not "pick the biggest share". **Itchy:** The rule is: **pick a covariate whose within-group variation is a thing that happens, not a thing you did.** Then check that its share is large enough to estimate from. Mass passes both. So today's covariate is **mass**, and today's question is: when a bird is heavier, is its wing measured longer, and **by the same amount in every bird**? Whether the up-and-down is real or is what three points do when you join them is the content of the hour. ### The slope you have been sharing **Itchy:** Two fits, in order of how much they let the birds get away with. Last week it went up. **Itchy:** Last week it went up, and last week I told you it would not always. Read the third column. **Toto:** The residual standard deviation collapsed. **Itchy:** From 2.1253 millimetres to 1.1256, which is a factor of 3.6 in residual *variance*. **Two things happen at once when you add `(1 | g)`**: you stop counting repeated measurements as fresh evidence, which pushes the standard error up, and you take an enormous amount of noise out of the residual, which pulls it down. Class 6 showed you the first one winning, on a predictor that barely moves within a bird. Which one wins is not settled by which side of one half the within-share falls on — mass is 58\.2% between-bird, and the second still wins: the standard error falls to 0.936 of what it was, a cut of 6\.4%. Keep the two mechanisms; do not keep an arithmetic test. **Toto:** And the slope halved. **Itchy:** The slope more than halved, from 0.443 to 0.1844 millimetres of wing per gram, which is a bigger move than anything Class 6 showed you. That is the second thing this predictor is doing, and it is bigger than today's subject. The pooled line is answering a blend of two questions — heavier birds are bigger birds, and a given bird gains and loses mass — and putting a bird term in the model changes the blend without separating it. **We will separate it, on this page, in the last section of the class.** Everything between here and there is fitted on the blended model, and the last section shows you which numbers move when we pull it apart. ### Freeing the slope > **μ_ij = (β0 + u_0j) + (β1 + u_1j) x_ij, with (u_0j, u_1j) ~ N(0, Σ) and y_ij ~ N(μ_ij, σ²)** > > **Σ = [σ_0², ρ σ_0 σ_1 ; ρ σ_0 σ_1, σ_1²]** **Itchy:** Measurement *i* on bird *j*, and the same six symbols as Class 6 with two additions. u_0j is the bird's own nudge to the intercept, which is exactly last week's u_j. u_1j is the bird's own nudge to the **slope**, and it is new. They are drawn together, from a two-dimensional normal, so there are three numbers in Σ rather than one: σ_0 the spread of intercepts, σ_1 the spread of slopes, and ρ the correlation between a bird's intercept and its slope. **Eddie:** Three numbers, and the model gained two parameters rather than one. **Itchy:** Two: σ_1 and ρ. Remember that, because it is what the test is testing. Report ρ with the origin in the same sentence, or do not report it. - **Centre a covariate whose zero is outside its range, every time.** With a far-away origin the fit can fail outright — an arithmetic failure in the optimiser, not a boundary — and centring removes it without changing the model. - **Shrinkage, now for slopes.** A group's predicted slope is pulled hard towards the population slope when the group has few measurements or little spread in *x*; here groups keep about 25% of the slope their own points suggest, and the spread of the predictions is not σ_1. - **Testing σ_1 = 0 is a boundary problem, and the mixture matters.** The naive χ²(2) is conservative. Stram and Lee's (1994) result covers exactly this step, *q* random effects against *q* + 1, and gives a fifty-fifty mixture of χ²(1) and χ²(2); read the assumptions of any correction before you take its p-value. - **Marginal residuals again.** `fitted` and `residuals` on these fits are population-level, so a quantile residual comes out about 2.1 times too wide; subtract *both* of the group's own numbers for the conditional residual, and read its worm plot for shape, not for σ, because shrinkage leaves part of each group effect behind. - **Never read a worm plot through a standardiser the outliers helped to set.** Find the rows far from their own group first, name them, and divide by a spread they cannot move. - **A coefficient on a repeated-measures covariate is a blend of two slopes, and splitting them costs one parameter.** Here the between-bird slope was 0.583 and the within-bird slope 0.049, and the split bought more AIC for one parameter than the random slope bought for two. - **A random slope on an unsplit covariate does two jobs.** Its variance absorbs the between-versus-within contrast the fixed part refused to separate; separating them cut σ_1 by 41% and the random slope survived. **Fit the decomposition first; then ask whether the within slope varies.** - **Maximal or parsimonious.** Barr et al. (2013) argue for the maximal random-effects structure; Bates et al. (2015) argue that over-parameterised structures should be reduced. This chapter is a small worked example: the maximal model wins by AIC, and most of the case for it evaporated when the fixed part was specified properly. ### Julia stuff - `@formula(y ~ x + (1 + x|g))`: the random slope. Everything else about the call is unchanged from Class 6, including the `bf` box and the positional family. - `vc(fit)`: the accessor for a correlated random-effect block. Returns a `Dict` of covariance matrices by grouping term; take `sqrt` of the diagonal for the standard deviations and divide the off-diagonal by their product for the correlation. What the printed block is, and why `re_sd` is empty for this fit, is in [Where the engine stops](appendix-b-engine.html). - `ranef(fit)[:g]`: for a random-slope fit, a matrix of groups by terms — intercept deviations in column one, slope deviations in column two, in the order of `sort(unique(df.g))`. - `aic(fit)`, `loglik(fit)`: the cheap comparison, and the ingredient of the test. - `lrtest(reduced, full)`: the naive likelihood-ratio test. It warns, correctly, when the extra parameters include a variance component. The Stram and Lee mixture for a random slope is `0.5 * ccdf(Chisq(1), stat) + 0.5 * ccdf(Chisq(2), stat)`, one line of `Distributions`. - `residuals(fit; type = :quantile, rng = MersenneTwister(seed))`: randomised quantile residuals, seeded in the cell; on a mixed fit they are marginal. --- ## Further reading *Graded by depth.
